On-Chain Operator. Lesson 10.7, Being the house: perp-exchange liquidity vaults. Navy and cyan. One idea at a time. You write it down. Education only.
You already split base yield from emissions. Advanced yield still starts with that split, then names a more particular engine.
Many on-chain perp exchanges let you deposit into a liquidity vault that acts as the counterparty to traders (the "house").
The vault earns trading fees, borrowing/funding fees and part of liquidations, and loses when traders win.

Risks: a run of profitable traders (or a few very large ones), open interest concentrated on one side, oracle manipulation or latency, the market-making strategy of the vault (some vaults actively trade), and exchange contract risk.
Check: the vault's historical P&L split (fees vs trader P&L), its open-interest caps, how it prices assets (oracle), and withdrawal rules (cooldowns, fees).
Work the example on paper. A vault shows 25% APR: 18% from fees, 7% from traders' net losses over the last 6 months. Stamp it Example. It is not a level to copy onto a live position.

Work the example on paper. In a strong one-directional trend, traders who are long win, so the vault's "trader P&L" component can swing to −20% or worse, wiping out the fees. Stamp it Example. It is not a level to copy onto a live position.

Work the example on paper. Size it as an active trading exposure, not as fixed income, and check whether withdrawals are delayed in stress. Stamp it Example. It is not a level to copy onto a live position.

Check yourself. 1. When does a perp liquidity vault lose money? The answer: When traders are net profitable, e.g. in strong trends.
Check yourself. 2. Why isn't it fixed income? The answer: Part of the return is traders' losses, which can reverse sharply.
Check yourself. 3. Name two things to check before depositing. The answer: Any two: fee vs trader-P&L history, OI caps, oracle design, withdrawal rules, contract risk.
